draft.title: Section 109
card: Section 109 of the Commonwealth Constitution deals with a clash between a state law and a Commonwealth law. It applies only when both laws are valid and cover the same matter.
If the two laws are inconsistent, the Commonwealth law prevails. The state law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency.
Only the part that clashes is invalid. The rest of the state law stays in force, and the state law is not repealed.
Laws can be inconsistent when it is impossible to obey both. They can also be inconsistent when the Commonwealth law is meant to cover the whole field, leaving no room for a state law.
draft.remember: If valid Commonwealth and state laws clash, the Commonwealth law wins and the state law is invalid to that extent.

a.q: A valid state law and a valid Commonwealth law on the same matter are inconsistent. What is the effect under section 109?
opts: The state law is invalid to the extent of the clash
The whole state law is repealed by the Commonwealth
The state law wins because the state acted first
Both laws are invalid until the High Court rules
a.why: Section 109 makes the Commonwealth law prevail, and the state law is invalid only to the extent of the inconsistency. It is not repealed, and the rest of it stays in force. The idea that the whole state law is repealed is tempting, but the card says only the clashing part is affected.
a.clue: Think about which law prevails and how much of the other is affected.

b.q: A valid Commonwealth law says a worker must be paid at least a set weekly amount. A valid Victorian law sets a lower amount for the same job and also sets rules on rest breaks, which the Commonwealth law does not cover. What is the result?
opts: The pay rule is invalid, but the rest break rules remain
The whole Victorian law is invalid, including rest breaks
The Victorian law wins on pay because it is more specific
Both pay rules apply, and the employer chooses between them
b.why: The two pay rules clash, so the Commonwealth rule prevails and the Victorian pay rule is invalid to that extent. The rest break rules do not clash with anything, so they stay in force. Striking down the whole Victorian law is tempting, but section 109 reaches only the inconsistent part.
b.clue: Only the part that clashes is affected.

a.best: The state law is invalid to the extent of the clash

b.best: The pay rule is invalid, but the rest break rules remain

problems.detail: The scenario does not fit the card's tests for inconsistency. If the Victorian law sets a lower minimum, an employer can obey both laws by paying the higher Commonwealth amount, so it is not 'impossible to obey both'. The question also does not say the Commonwealth law covers the field. The clash really rests on the 'alter, impair or detract' idea (as in Clyde Engineering v Cowburn), which the card does not teach. Reword so the laws cannot both be obeyed, for example a Victorian law that says the worker must be paid no more than a lower amount, or state that the Commonwealth law is meant to cover the whole field of pay.

check.summary: The card and question a are accurate. Question b's minimum-pay example can be obeyed under both laws, so by the card's own tests it is not clearly an inconsistency. Reword it so the pay rules cannot both be obeyed.
